(D) is true: \(L\) plays the role of inertia, since \(\tfrac{1}{2}LI^{2}\) is the analogue of \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\). authoredSolutions.2: Push the floating cube down by \(x\); the extra buoyant force is the restoring force \[F = -\rho g A x,\qquad A = L^{2} = (0.1)^{2} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}.\] So the force constant is \[k = \rho g A = 10^{3}\times 10 \times 10^{-2} = 100\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}.\] With \(m = 10\ \mathrm{g} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{kg}\), \[T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{10^{-2}}{100}} = 2\pi \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s}.\] Comparing with \(y\pi \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s}\) gives \(y = 2\), so the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.3: Statement-I: the viscosity of water falls sharply as temperature rises, so for the same driving pressure hot water flows faster than cold water. Statement-I is true. So soap water has a lower, not higher, surface tension than fresh water, and Statement-II is false. Hence the correct choice is B.

authoredSolutions.11: The axial field of dipole 1 and the equatorial field of dipole 2 are collinear and oppositely directed at \(P\), so a null requires equal magnitudes. With \(p = 2aq\) the EXACT (non-ideal) fields are \[E_{\text{axial}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{2pr}{\left( r^{2}-a^{2} \right)^{2}},\qquad E_{\text{equatorial}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{p}{\left( r^{2}+a^{2} \right)^{3/2}}.\] Note that in the ideal-dipole limit these reduce to \(2kp/r^{3}\) and \(kp/r^{3}\), which can never cancel -- so the balance can only occur where \(a\) is comparable to (or larger than) \(r\). Setting the two equal, \[2r\left( r^{2}+a^{2} \right)^{3/2} = \left( r^{2}-a^{2} \right)^{2}.\] Dividing by \(r^{4}\) and writing \(t = a/r\), \[2\left( 1+t^{2} \right)^{3/2} = \left( t^{2}-1 \right)^{2}.\] Testing \(t = 3\): the left side is \(2(10)^{3/2} = 63.2\) and the right side is \((9-1)^{2} = 64\) -- equal to about \(1\%\) (the exact root is \(t \approx 2.98\)).
